what_it_does: This paper demonstrates something unusual: a self-propelled robot built entirely on a single silicon chip using standard CMOS manufacturing (the process used for mainstream integrated circuits). The challenge is integrating three capabilities on one die: harvesting energy from the environment, generating control signals, and actually moving. Previous chip-embedded robots either relied on external magnetic coupling (which is inefficient and requires specialized components) or needed custom fabrication incompatible with standard chip production. This design uses two elegant on-chip mechanisms working in tandem. For energy harvesting, it employs parity-time symmetry (a physics concept where loss and gain are balanced)—a resonant structure tuned to sub-GHz radio frequencies that captures ambient electromagnetic energy at those frequencies. For propulsion, it uses traveling-wave electroosmosis: controlled electrical fields create tiny electrostatic forces in microscale fluid channels on the chip surface, generating locomotion. All power comes from the harvested energy, so no battery is needed.
